title: Chapter 6 — That Democratic Institutions And Manners Tend To Raise Rents And Shorten The Terms Of Leases
paragraphs: And Shorten The Terms Of Leases

What has been said of servants and masters applies, to a certain extent, to landowners and tenant farmers; but this subject deserves to be considered on its own. In America there are, properly speaking, no tenant farmers; every man owns the ground he tills. It must be admitted that democratic laws tend greatly to increase the number of landowners and to reduce the number of tenants. Yet what happens in the United States is much less attributable to the institutions of the country than to the country itself. In America land is cheap, and anyone can easily become a landowner; its returns are small, and its produce cannot well be divided between a landowner and a farmer. America therefore stands alone in this, as in many other respects, and it would be a mistake to take it as a model.

I believe that in democratic as well as in aristocratic countries there will be landowners and tenants, but the connection between them will be of a different kind. In aristocracies the rent of a farm is paid to the landlord not only in money, but in respect, regard, and duty; in democracies the whole is paid in cash. When estates are divided and passed from hand to hand, and the permanent connection that existed between families and the soil is dissolved, the landowner and the tenant are brought together only casually. They meet for a moment to settle the terms of the agreement, and then lose sight of each other. They are two strangers drawn together by a common interest, who keenly discuss a matter of business whose sole object is to make money.

As property is subdivided and wealth distributed across the country, the community fills with people whose former wealth is in decline, and with others whose fortunes are of recent growth and whose needs grow faster than their resources. For all such people the smallest monetary profit matters, and none of them feels disposed to waive any of his claims or forgo any portion of his income. As ranks are intermingled, and as very large as well as very small fortunes become rarer, each day brings the social condition of the landowner closer to that of the farmer. One has no natural, uncontested superiority over the other; between two men who are equals, and not comfortable in their circumstances, the contract of rent is purely a matter of money. A man whose estate stretches over a whole district, and who owns a hundred farms, is well aware of the importance of winning the affection of several thousand men at the same time; this object seems to call for his efforts, and to attain it he will readily make considerable sacrifices. But the man who owns a hundred acres is insensible to such considerations, and cares very little about winning the private regard of his tenant.

An aristocracy does not expire like a man in a single day; the aristocratic principle is slowly undermined in men's opinion before it is attacked in their laws. Long before open war is declared against it, the tie that had until then united the higher classes to the lower can be seen gradually loosening. Indifference and contempt are shown by one class, jealousy and hatred by the others; the intercourse between rich and poor becomes less frequent and less kindly, and rents are raised. This is not the consequence of a democratic revolution, but its certain harbinger; for an aristocracy that has lost the affections of the people, once and for all, is like a tree dead at the root, the more easily torn up by the winds the higher its branches have spread.

In the course of the last fifty years the rents of farms have increased amazingly, not only in France but throughout most of Europe. The remarkable improvements that have taken place in agriculture and manufactures during the same period are not enough, in my opinion, to explain this fact; recourse must be had to another cause, more powerful and more hidden. I believe that cause is to be found in the democratic institutions that several European nations have adopted, and in the democratic passions that more or less agitate all the rest. I have often heard great English landowners congratulate themselves that today they draw a much larger income from their estates than their fathers did. They may have good reason to be glad; but they certainly do not know what they are glad of. They think they are making a clear gain when in reality they are only making an exchange; what they are parting with for cash is their influence, and what they gain in money will soon be lost in power.

There is yet another sign by which it is easy to know that a great democratic revolution is underway or approaching. In the Middle Ages almost all lands were leased for lives, or for very long terms; the domestic economy of that period shows that leases for ninety-nine years were more frequent then than twelve-year leases are now. Men then believed that families were immortal; their conditions seemed settled forever, and the whole of society appeared so fixed that no one supposed anything would ever be stirred or shaken in its structure. In ages of equality, the human mind takes a different bent; the prevailing notion is that nothing lasts, and man is haunted by the thought of change. Under this impression, both the landowner and the tenant are instinctively averse to long terms of obligation; they are afraid of being tied tomorrow by the contract that benefits them today. They have vague forebodings of some sudden and unforeseen change in their circumstances; they mistrust themselves; they fear lest their tastes change, and they will come to regret not being able to rid themselves of what they had coveted. Nor are such fears unfounded, for in democratic ages, that which fluctuates most amid the fluctuation of all around is the heart of man.
